blocks.text: A Square. On one side, the Palace of the Commandant; on the other, an Hotel with a Balcony. Time, Daybreak.
Leporello; afterwards Don Juan and Donna Anna.

lines: Thus I’m tortured night and day,
And no thanks I ever get;
Now I’m chill’d by piercing winds,
Now with rain I’m dripping wet.
I’m resolv’d to change my state,
And be a gentleman so great;
Yes, yes, yes, and be a gentleman so great.
I’ve a precious master truly;
While within he woos the ladies,
I must sentinel without be!
I’m resolv’d to change my state,
And be a gentleman so great.
Softly now, there’s someone coming,
And I must not here be seen.

blocks.text: Enter Don Juan, followed by Donna Anna.

lines: Till thy name I’ve learned, thou viper,
From this spot thou shalt not go.
Foolish girl, beware my fury!
Who I am thou ne’er shalt know.
(What a tumult! oh, dear, what screaming)
My master’s in some trouble new!
(Be silent, or my rage you’ll rue.)
Miscreant!
Imprudent woman!
Villain, tremble! Help! what, ho!
I’m desperate,
And my persecutor fain would know.
(Some fearful act she’ll surely
Make me do.)
(Some fearful act! and I
Must share it, too.)

blocks.text: Don Juan, the Commandant, and Leporello.

lines: Unhand her, villain;
Turn and defend thee.
Hence, fool! I deign not
With thee to combat.
Dost thou fear me?
Dost from me fly?
(I wish I could—
I think I’ll try.)
Coward!
Tremble! for thou must
Most surely die.
Ah, great Heaven! Powers of Mercy!
’Neath t’ assassin’s hand expiring,
Forth, from out my quiv’ring bosom,
Fast the life-blood wells away.
There the meddling fool lies prostrate:
Agony his frame is wringing;
Fast his soul its flight is winging,
As his life-blood wells away.
(Horror, horror! deed of darkness!
Terror dire, my blood congealing,
Through my veins like ice ’tis stealing—
I know not what to do or to say.)

blocks.text: Here, master, to my disgrace; and you—
Oh! which is dead—you or the old man?
Two pretty exploits, truly, for one night: seduce the daughter, and kill the father!
He was bent on his ruin.
And was Donna Anna bent on her’s?
Silence! Question not, but follow me;—breathe not a word, or—
I won’t, I won’t, Sir! I’ll never speak again.
Donna Anna, Don Octavio, and Servants with torches.
Ah, my father is in danger! let us fly to his succor.
To the last drop of my blood you may command me. But where is the villain?
Seeing the body of her Father.
But, just Heaven, what sight of horror presents itself! My father! my dear father!
Ah, he is slain! This blood, these wounds—his face cover’d with the pale hue of death! He no longer breathes—his limbs are cold. My father! my dear, my beloved father! I faint—I die!
Hasten, my friends, to assist your unfortunate mistress! Fetch water, scents—try all means to restore her. Hasten, I entreat you! Donna Anna, beloved mistress! Her grief, I fear, is fatal.
Quickly remove her from this scene of horror. Console thee, love! oh, cease this sorrow!

lines: Leave me, for ever leave me!
Heaven of life bereave me!
With him who being gave me,
Oh, let me perish too!
Forbear this wild appealing!
Oh, calm your frantic feeling!
And hear your lover, kneeling,
Who lives alone for you!
My love, alas! forgive me!
My madd’ning mind will leave me!
My father, thee I call!
Console thee, soothe thy mind, love
Ever in me thou’lt find, love,
A father, lover, all!
Swear for my bleeding sire
Thou’lt stern avenger prove.
I swear by thine eyes’ soft fire!
I swear by all our love!
Oh, moment full of anguish,
That such an oath makes needful!
Our hearts with grief still languish,—
Our cup’s with sorrow full!

blocks.text: Come, then, out with this mystery—what is it?
The affair I am about to speak of is of consequence.
Better and better. To the point, then.
Promise me not be in a passion.
I give you my honor, provided it does not relate to the Commandant.
But may I speak my whole mind freely?
Well, since you give me leave, dear master, I must say that the life you lead is horrible, and the sooner you amend it—
What, rascal! do you dare to talk to me thus?
No more, knave! Promise or no promise, be silent, or—
I am dumb! I say nothing, dear master.
It is the way to keep us friends. Now, hark ye, Leporello: do you know what brings me here?
I know nothing, but I guess it’s some new love affair: you must tell me the lady’s name, that I may put it in my list.

Spoken like a clever fellow! Know, then, that I am enamor’d of a most beautiful woman, and I am sure she returns my love. I have seen her and conversed with her: she is to meet me to-night at the Casino; but hush! a female approaches.
Zooks! what an exquisite ear he has!
At the first glance I see she is handsome.
With an eye like a hawk!
Let us retire a little, and reconnoitre.
Donna Elvira; Don Juan and Leporello concealed.

lines: Ah! how shall I discover
Where this barbarian lives?
Though I may not call him mine,
My heart still homage gives.
But should I find the traitor,
And find he loves no more,
’Twill then be mine to torture,
And wound his bosom’s core.

blocks.text: Do you hear? This fair damsel is complaining of some faithless lover. Poor girl! I must seek to console her.
He has consol’d, in this manner one thousand and eight hundred only!
What do I see? Don Juan! Monster, robber, mountain of deceit!
What choice epithets! One may see that she is an old acquaintance.
Come, dear Elvira, restrain this anger! Hear me—let me speak!

What can you say in excuse for your black conduct? To enter secretly my house, and, by artifice, by oaths and flattery, to become master of my affections! To make me your wife, and then, defying Heaven and earth, as it were,—denying my sacred right,—and with unheard of treachery departing, in three days, from Burgos. To fly, to abandon me—to leave me a prey to remorse and anguish! A sad return for having lov’d so well!
This is as true as if it was printed!
Yes, I confess it all; but know, Elvira, that I had my strong reasons for this;
What can they be but levity and want of faith? But heaven has permitted me to discover you, that I may avenge its wrongs, and my own.
My dearest Elvira, be a little more rational, I entreat you!
If you will not believe me, you will at least believe this worthy gentleman.
You will explain the whole to her.
Yes, yes, you will explain all.
Madam—assuredly—in the strange world in which we live—it may—be safely asserted—that a square is not a circle—and, therefore—
Abominable villain! is my grief a fit subject for mockery? And you, Don Juan—
Turns, and discovers that he has gone.
Heaven! the reprobate has left me! Unhappy me! what shall I do? Which way did he go?
Ah, let him go! He does not deserve that you should bestow a thought upon him.

Do not be unhappy! You are not the first lady he has deserted, neither will you be the last. See, here is a large book: it is filled entirely with the names of his mistresses. Every country, every city—nay, every village, has witnessed his exploits in gallantry!

lines: Pray behold, ma’am!
In this long list I’ve made, is
An account of my master’s fair ladies!
Not Jove so renown’d for his trade is:
Pray observe it, and read it with me!
First in Italy, ma’am, seven hundred,
Then in Germany, eight may be number’d;
Then in Turkey and France, one and ninety,
But, but, in Spain, ma’am,
One thousand and three!
Here are chambermaids by dozens.
City dames and country cousins;
Countesses and Baronesses,
Marchionesses and Princesses,
All descriptions, ages, classes,
Not a woman could go free.
First the fair ones he bewitches
By the softness of his speeches,—
Makes the brown ones in a fever,
Warmly vowing love for ever!
With the pale ones he will languish,
Melt and sigh in tender anguish;
The great and tall ones sometimes warm him,
High and low, ma’am, old and young, ma’am,
Own the music of his tongue, ma’am:
Though, if I must tell the truth, ma’am,
I know he’d give the choice to youth, ma’am,
But ugly, pretty, fat, or thin—
Something a petticoat within!
It matters not, for, short or tall,
’Tis very plain he loves them all!

blocks.text: Am I thus become the victim of perfidy? and is this the return for all my affection? but my wrongs shall not go unpunished! Before he escapes me, let the arm of justice—Love sleeps in my breast; I feel but rage and hatred.
The country with a view of Don Juan’s Palace.
Zerlina; Masetto. Male and Female Peasants.

lines: Pretty lasses, love’s summer, remember,
Ever flies upon gossamer wing;
Suffer not, then, life’s chilly December
To destroy Cupid’s bow and his string!
La la la, la la la!
But make haste and be happy like me.
Ah, But make haste and be happy,
Like thee, la la la lira.
And, ye lads who are constantly changing,
For a time though ’tis pleasant to run
From this beauty to that, ever ranging,
Yet, at last, pray be constant to one!
Lira, lira la!
And be happy, be happy, like me!
Lira la, lira la!
And be happy, be happy like thee!
Oh, what rapture! the marriage-bells ringing,
To be dancing and playing and singing!
Who so happy, so happy as we!
Lira la, lira la!
Who so happy, so happy as we!

blocks.text: Heaven be praised, she is gone! But look, look, what a lively group! What pretty girls!
(Faith! among so many, one or two may fall to my share.)
Friends, good day! Pray go on with your sports, your singing and dancing. Is this a wedding?
Yes, my lord; and I am the bride.
I give you joy. Where is the bridegroom?
Here, my lord, at your service.
Very good! at my service! Spoken like a youth of spirit.
It is enough to be the husband.
Oh, my dear Masetto has such an excellent heart!
And so have I, be assur’d; that is why we should be friends. And your name?
Ah my dear Masetto! my dear Zerlina! accept my protection. Leporello! what are you doing there, knave?
Who is making love to some of the women.
I too, master, am making an offer of my protection.

Instantly conduct these happy people to my palace: give orders to supply them with coffee, chocolate, wine, sweetmeats—do your best to entertain them. Show them the gardens, the gallery, the hall; and above all, pay particular attention to my dear Masetto. Do you understand?
I understand. Friends, let us go.
My Zerlina cannot stay here without me.
His lordship will well supply your place—he knows how to play your part to perfection.
Fear not, Zerlina is in the care of a nobleman. Go, then; she shall soon follow with me.
Go; fear nothing: I am in the care of a nobleman.
For that reason you have nothing to fear.
Oh, reply no more! If without more words, you do not immediately depart, Masetto, you shall repent it.

Yes, my lord, I understand you! and, since you are pleas’d to command my absence, will go without farther reply. You say you are a nobleman, and I cannot doubt your word, but something within tells me that your designs are not honorable.
Traitress! viper! you were born to be my ruin!
Ay now! do stay! It is quite prudent in you to trust him; let my lord here make a lady of you.
At length, my sweet Zerlina, we are rid of this troublesome fellow. Say, then, my angel, have I not well contriv’d?
My lord, he is my lover.
What! he? Do you think that a nobleman, a man of rank, as I am, can suffer such bewitching beauty to be profaned by a base clown?
But, my lord, I have promis’d to marry him.

Such a promise is void in itself; you were not born to be the wife of a country booby. Those roguish eyes, those pouting lips, those pretty little fingers, so white and tapering, ensure you a better fortune.
Not like to be imposed on. I have heard that noblemen are seldom frank and sincere with women.
It is a vile calumny of the vulgar: nobility and honor always go together. But do not let us lose time: this very moment I will marry you.
Certainly. That house you see is mine: there we shall be alone; and there, my angel, we will be married.

lines: Then with thy hand in mine, dear,
Thou’lt whisper gently yes!
The castle’s lord be thine, dear,
Come, and thy lover bless!
I would, and yet I would not;
My breast with terror heaves:
’Twould be the happiest lot,
Unless this lord deceives.
Come, then, with me, my beauty!
Masetto claims my duty.
I wish to change thy state, love.
I yield myself to fate, love.
Come, then! Then with thy hand in mine, dear,
Thou’lt whisper gently yes!
I would, and yet I would not;
My breast with terror heaves.
Then come, and share with me the pleasure
Of innocence and love.

blocks.text: Stay, wicked one, stay! Heaven has permitted me to overhear your perfidious design; and I may yet save this poor artless girl from your barbarian grasp.
Oh, me! what is it I hear?
My love, do you not see that I am amusing myself?
Amusing yourself! Yes, cruel man, I know too well how you amuse yourself.
But, my lord, does this lady speak truly?
This poor forlorn damsel almost adores me, and I cannot but seem, out of pity, to return her love, for I am so tender-hearted; that is my only misfortune.

Oh, Heaven! into what excesses, into what horrible, unheard-of crimes is this wretched man plunged! The wrath of Heaven can no longer be averted. Already I see the fatal bolt launched at his devoted head,—already I see the abyss opened beneath him.

lines: Hapless Elvira!
What contending feelings agitate my bosom!
Why these sighs? what checks my utterance?
Though by him I’ve been neglected,
Though my peace has fled, alas!
Though his falseness I’ve detected,
Prayers for him my lips still pass.
When I think on wrongs I’m bearing
Vengeance only steels my heart;
When I see him perils sharing,
I’d avert the poison’d dart.

blocks.text: Don Juan, Don Octavio, Donna Anna; afterwards Donna Elvira.
My evil genius seems to take pleasure to-day in crossing all my pleasant schemes—everything goes wrong.
Dearest Donna Anna, cease these unavailing tears! Let us think only of vengeance. Ah, Don Juan here!
Ah, at length we have found you! Have you, my friend, a noble, a generous heart!
I wonder whether my ill stars have put any suspicion into her head?
What a question, Madame! wherefore do you ask it?
We have need of all your friendship and advice.
Pray command me,—command my relations, my friends; this arm, this sword, shall be devoted to your service. But fairest Donna, why these tears? What wretch has dared disturb thy bosom’s wonted calm?
Ha! do I find you again, perfidious monster!

lines: Oh, list not to those witching tones!
They come not from the heart!
On me they fell but to betray—
He’ll play on thee that part.
Oh, Heaven! what beauty’s in that form!
What softness and what grace!
Her patient grief, her looks forlorn,
In my fond heart find place.
My friends, this poor young creature
For love of me, raves wildly:
Leave her to me, oh leave her
With her I’ll reason mildly.
Ah do not heed! his words are false!
She’s frantic; don’t believe her.
Stay, false one! nor deceive her.
Oh, which shall we believe?
(I feel around my heart now stealing
Hopeless love, disdain, revealing
That this fair unhappy lady
Suffers more than words can tell.)
(Despair around my heart now stealing
Hopeless love, disdain, revealing
That on earth I still shall ever
Suffer more than words can tell.)
Hence I will not now depart,
Till I hear the truth of this.
There’s no madness in her manner,
And her words are not amiss.
(If I go now, their blind anger
On me may suspicion turn.)
From his face malign, now judge how
Justly does my fury burn.
This poor lady?
Reason fails her.
This young signor?
Is a traitor.
Go, unhappy!
Base deceiver!
Already I begin to doubt.
Softly, softly, I beseech you!
People see who come this way;
Prythee have a little prudence—
Silence keep, and go away.
Hope it not, thou perjur’d traitor!
Prudence certainly hath left me—
You of that have quite bereft me:
I’ll expose you, come what may.
Ah, how alter’d, see his manner!
What a change! what calm submission!
This, indeed, the truth disclosing,
Now to me doth all betray.
Unhappy lady! I must follow her
And watch her footsteps, lest in evil hour
Some desp’rate act she dare. Excuse me, then,
Most charming Donna Anna:
If there is any service I can render,
I shall be found at home. My friends, farewell!
Don Octavio, I’m confounded.
What has happen’d?
For pity’s sake, support me!
My love, take courage.
Oh, Heav’n! he is the murderer of my father!
What is’t you say?
Yes, I can doubt no more. His last few words—
His voice, form, accent, brought back to my mind
The image of the villain who had dar’d,
At night, in my apartment—
Heavens! can it be,
That, under friendship’s sacred guise, the wretch—
But how was this? Relate to me
At once, the fearful tale.
Already far advanc’d
Was then the night,
When, sitting in my room, and quite alone,
As chance would have it, lo! I saw then enter
Wrapp’d in a mantle,
A man, whom at the first moment
I took for you;
But soon perceiv’d
That a mistake I’d made.
The wretch! Proceed.
Silently he nearer came,
And clasp’d me in his arms: I shriek’d,
And tried to free myself, the more he press’d me;
But no one came; then with one hand
My voice he sought to stifle,
And with the other grasp’d me
So forcibly, I gave me up for lost.
Villain! and then!
Grief and despair at last
Gave me new strength against
This infamous attempt; after a struggle
I disengaged myself,
And broke away.
Again I breathe!
Then
My cries I still renew’d, I call’d for help—
The villain fled, and instantly I follow’d,
Even to the street, to stop him; and I now
Became the assailant, who was once th’ assail’d
My father ran to aid me and detect him,
But the old man, being weaker than his foe,
Was overpower’d, alas! and met his doom.
Thou know’st who it was that attempted mine honor,
And who was the traitor my father that slew
’Tis vengeance I ask for—thy heart claims it too.
Remember the earth with his sacred blood stain’d—
Remember his wound, for it calls from the tomb,
If thy zeal should relax; and let death be his doom.
Could I ever have believ’d
That a gallant cavalier
Should the perpetrator be
Of such a crime as now I heard?
Let me leave no means untried
To learn the truth; for, as her lover,
My heart now tells me that I ought
To undeceive or to avenge her.
For on her happiness mine is dependant—
Whatever delights her, to me giveth joy:
Were her life misery, mine ’twould destroy;
And to her ev’ry sigh mine doth reply;
Mine is her vengeance, and mine are her tears—
I share her sorrows, her hopes, and her fears.
Whate’er may be the consequence, I must
Leave this wild rake.
Yonder he comes: behold
With what a careless air he moves along.
Well, my little Leporello, does all go well?
No, my little Don Juan, all goes ill.
How? all goes ill?
I went to the house
As you directed me.
With all those people.
Very well!
By chatting with them,—
By leading them to pastimes, and with fibs,
That I have learn’d so well in serving you,
I tried to amuse them.
Very good!
I said
A thousand things to pacify Masetto,
And lead him from the thought of jealousy.
’Tis well, upon my word.
I set both men and women drinking;
They were already half inebriate:
Some sung, and others sported—
The rest went drinking on: all was going well,
When, who do you think, arriv’d?
Zerlina.
Right!
And with her, who came also?
Donna Elvira.
Right! and she spoke of you.
All the evil that her lips could utter?
True, upon my word.
And what said you?
Nothing.
And she—
Continued her abuse.
While you?
When it appear’d to me
That she was almost tir’d, I gently led her
Out of the garden, and then dexterously
I closed the door and lock’d it—stealing off,
I left her in the street, standing alone.
Excellent! most excellent!
The affair could not go better; you have begun,
And I know how to finish.
These pretty country girls bewitch my heart:
I wish to entertain them till the night.
Now that they’re merry
With port or with sherry,
A feast, do not tarry,
Go and prepare;
If by-the-by, too
Nice girls you spy, too,
Quick, have an eye to
Let them be there;
Trumpets affrighting,
Waltzes inviting,
Minuets delighting,
Frolic and fun here,
French, English, German,
Bring far and near;
Minuets delighting
All who appear.
Frolics and feasting
All hearts to cheer.
While I go prying,
Pretty girls eyeing,
Tenderly sighing
Till they are won.
Many tomorrow,
Not to my sorrow,
You’ll add to the list of ladies I’ve won.

blocks.text: A Rural Prospect. On one side, the Palace of Don Juan; on the other, a Pavilion.

lines: Masetto, listen a moment! Masetto, I say!
Do not come near me.
And why?
Faithless! could I endure the touch
Of a false hand like thine?
Ah, me! hush, cruel man!
From thee I’ve not deserved such treatment.
How! are you bold enough to make excuses
To remain alone with a man? and to leave
Even on our wedding day—with infamy
To brand the forehead of an honest man,
And stain his name with shame! Ah, were not
That I consider what the world would say.
But if I’m not in fault—if he deceiv’d me?
And then what fear you? Nay,
Be calm, my life!
He did not touch me with a finger’s tip.
Will you not now believe me, cruel man?
Come here, exhaust your rage, and take my life—
Do with me what you will; but then, Masetto,
Then, I entreat you, let’s be friends again!
Chide me, chide me, dear Masetto,
Chide Zerlina at your will;
Like the patient lamb I’ll suffer,
Meek and mute, and loving still.
Rend those locks you prais’d so highly;
From thine arms Zerlina cast;
These fond eyes in rage extinguish
Fondly still they’ll look their last.
Ah! I see, love, you’re relenting—
Pardon, kneeling, I implore ye!
Night and day, to thee devoted,
Here I vow to err no more.
This enchantress fair and shy
Soft persuasion now would try!
Men to be weak in mind have never ceas’d.

blocks.text: The same.—Don Juan (from without) and Servants.

lines: Let all be now prepar’d for a grand feast.
Ah, Masetto, Masetto! that is the voice
Of my lord the cavalier!
Well, what of that?
He will come hither.
Well, let him come.
Ah! had I but a loophole
To escape—
What do you fear?
Why do you thus turn pale? Ah, now I know!
I understand, false girl!
You are afraid I should discover
The secrets that have pass’d between you.
Quick, oh quick! before he comes,
In this corner I will hide:
In this nook I’ll stand conceal’d!—
Secret, silent, let me bide.
Hear me, hear me! oh, Masetto!
Do not hide yourself, but stay!
If he finds you, my poor fellow,
Who can tell what he may say?
Let him say or do his worst.
Ah! you heed not what I say!
Speak aloud, and here remain.
What folly now is in thy brain?
I shall know if she is faithful,
And how went this strange affair.
Oh, how cruel and ungrateful!
Thus he tries what I can dare.
Arise, enjoy yourselves like men!
Here we’ll laugh and dance a measure.
Cast off coyness, oh sweet girls!
Here we live for joy and pleasure.
In the hall prepar’d for dancing,
Let the ball with joy be crown’d;
And, amid the scene entrancing,
See the sparkling cup go round.
Arise, etc.
Conceal’d among these trees,
I, perhaps may pass unseen.
My charming, my graceful Zerlina!
I see you—you cannot escape!
Ah! I entreat you, let me go!
No, my angel, pray remain.
If you have one spark of pity!
Yes, my dearest, I’m all love,
Come with me, then, to this bower
And I there will make you bless’d.
Ah! if my jealous lover saw him
Well I know what he could do.
Masetto!
Yes, Masetto.
And why were you conceal’d there?
Your pretty girl, Zerlina—
She, poor maid, can no longer
Be happy without you.
My lord, I understand.
Come, then, let us merry be;
Quickly! the musicians see!
Come, dance at once with me.
Yes, let us all merry be,
And together go all three,
To join the rest, and dance.
Yes, let us all merry be, etc.

blocks.text: Donna Anna, Donna Elvira, and Don Octavio.

lines: Be firm, be firm, I pray you—
My good friends, I implore you;
And soon the guilty traitor
Shall for his crimes atone.
Elvira counsels wisely—
We must have courage, truly,
Then banish, oh my fair one!
Thy fear and terror soon.
The moments full of danger,
Some ill may yet befall;
I fear for thee, belov’d one—
I fear, indeed, for all.
My lord, look out a moment!
See what gay masks are here!
Invite them in, and beg them
To come and share our cheer.
See, see, that look, that voice,
Betray the traitor there!
Hist! hist! oh, maskers, hist.
Reply to him for us.
What is your pleasure, pray?
My lord entreats your presence
To honor this his home.
We thank him for this favor.
My fair companions, come.
My lord will quickly prove
If these fair dames can love.
Just Heav’n, our path protecting,
Oh, guide our steps aright!
Just Heav’n on him avenge me
Who all my hopes did blight!

blocks.text: A Ball-Room in the Palace of Don Juan.
Zerlina, Don Juan, Leporello, Masetto; Male and Female Peasants; Servants and Musicians.

lines: Rest awhile, pretty maids, from your dancing.
Come, refresh yourselves, gentlemen gay.
While around us bright eyes are thus glancing,
Who so happy, so happy as we!
Bring some coffee!
Chocolate, here!
Ah, Zerlina, pray take care!
Sherbet!
Some comfort!
Ah, Zerlina, pray beware!
See, the scene has made us glad;
But its end may yet be sad.
You are indeed charming, lovely Zerlina!
Your lordship is very polite.
The saucy girl makes holiday!
How pretty you are, Giannotta, Sadrina!
Touch her, I’ll knock your head off!
This Masetto’s gone out of his mind.
Sadly, I fear, this affair will end.
This Masetto’s gone out of his mind.
And, to win her, I must use all my skill.
Despair and rage my bosom will fill.

blocks.text: Donna Anna, Donna Elvira, Don Octavio. The same.

lines: Fair maskers, I entreat you,
Enter and join our ball.
My house to all is open,
And liberty for all.
We, my lord, most thankfully
Receive your hospitality.
Now, recommence the ball!
You marshal forth the dancing.
Come now, the gay throng joining,
Zerlina, dance with me.
Excellent! now for dancing.
That is the country girl.
Ah, how I tremble!
Conceal your alarm.
Everything goes well!
Yes, everything goes well.
Take care of friend Masetto.
He’s jealous, and won’t dance.
Zerlina, I’m your partner;
Come hither, come with me.
Come here, my friend Masetto,
And let us do as they.
No, no, I will not dance.
Nay, list to what I say.
I tell you, never—nay.
Yes, dear Masetto, pray.
I will not dance to-day.
Yet, let us dance, my friend:
With me their joys partake.
No longer I’ll pretend.
Nay, feign for pity’s sake!
Come, come with me, my love!
Leave me alone. Zerlina!
Come hither, quick, with me.
Oh, Heav’ns! I’m betray’d!
Some uproar sure will come.
He leads her to her ruin,
And rushes to his doom.
Help! help! Oh, aid me, aid me.
Let us aid the helpless girl.
Ah, Zerlina!
Villain, leave me!
Hark! from that side comes the voice.
Villain!
Let us burst the door!
Help me, friends! I faint, I die!
Here we’re ready to defend thee!

blocks.text: Re-entering with his Sword drawn, and turning to Leporello

lines: Here’s the wretch that did the wrong
But by my hand he shall die!
Villain, perish!
Why? oh why?
You shall die!
Yet stay! why should I?
Hope not, hope not thus to escape.
Vainly seeks he to deceive us—
Hoping thus the truth to hide.
Donna Elvira!
Yes, thou false one!
Don Octavio!
Yes, Signor!
Ah, believe me—
Oh, thou traitor.
Traitor! traitor!
Everything at length is known!
Tremble, traitor! wrath is waking!
Terror deep thy conscience shaking,
Sudden vengeance guilt o’ertaking—
Thou, unheard, for aid shalt cry.
Now my head is quite confounded:
What to do I do not know;
And by storms I am surrounded—
Menacing some sudden blow.
Dead to hope, unpity’d falling,
Wild remorse thy heart appalling,
Thou for mercy vainly calling,
In despairing guilt shall die!
Though the lightning’s round me flashing,
Though the thunder’s o’er me crashing,
Fiery bolts may on me fall—
Naught my courage shall appal!
